scenes.line1: Can't see where Azure traffic dies?
scenes.say: Ever wonder why your Azure VM can't reach a service, but you can't just plug into a switch to check? How do you actually prove where the traffic stops?

scenes.label: Watcher
scenes.sub: Network Watcher shows if traffic is allowed, and where it goes next.
scenes.say: Network Watcher is your go-to tool. It tells you if traffic is allowed, and where it would go, without any guesswork.

rows.b: See real security rules on the NIC
Test if a connection would be allowed
Find the next device traffic hits

scenes.say: First, look at the effective security rules on the network card. Then, use IP Flow Verify to check if a connection would be allowed. Next Hop shows the next device your traffic hits, and Effective Routes tells you what routes actually apply.

scenes.title: Diagnose with Azure CLI
scenes.say: You can use the Azure command line to run these checks. Test if a network security group allows the traffic, see where packets go next, list effective security rules, and test end-to-end connectivity.

scenes.question: What do you check after NSG rules?
scenes.right: Check the next hop and effective routes to see if traffic is routed or black-holed before looking at firewall logs.
scenes.say: Here's a common trap: After checking security group rules, don't jump straight to firewall logs. Always check the next hop and effective routes first. You might find traffic is black-holed before it even reaches a firewall.
